steps.title: The PC boots a small Linux on the Jetson, and that Linux does the writing
steps.body:
Time runs down the page. The left dashed line is the host PC, the right one is the Jetson, and each arrow is a message in one of seven numbered steps. Notes beside the lines say what each side is doing.

The PC never writes the storage directly. It loads a small Linux into the board's RAM, and that Linux pulls the images and writes them itself.

anchor: one USB-C cable: data only, and it also carries the Ethernet link (usb0)
steps.title: One USB-C cable is the only link
steps.body:
The host runs `sudo l4t_initrd_flash.sh`. The board sits in recovery mode, a state where its BootROM waits for a PC on USB.

The cable carries data only, no power, and later it also carries an Ethernet link called `usb0`. A bad cable breaks both the first and the later steps.

anchor: Force Recovery Mode: BootROM waits for USB
steps.title: Step 1: a jumper makes the BootROM wait for USB
steps.body:
With a jumper between REC and GND at power-on, only the BootROM has run: it waits on USB instead of loading firmware. On the PC, `lsusb -d 0955:` shows `0955:7523 NVidia Corp.`

If that device does not appear, nothing else can work, so check the jumper, cable and port first.

anchor: RCM boot: bootloader + kernel + initrd go into RAM
MB2 on the CPU complex loads
steps.title: Step 2: the host pushes a bootloader, kernel and initrd into RAM
steps.body:
The tool generates and runs `flash.sh --no-flash --rcm-boot`. RCM is the BootROM's recovery protocol for loading code over USB.

MB2 on the CPU complex loads the three pieces into SDRAM and starts them, so the board is now running a Linux that lives only in RAM.

anchor: a USB Ethernet link appears: usb0 (IPv6)
steps.title: Step 3: the cable becomes a network
steps.body:
The RAM-booted Linux exposes the USB cable as `usb0`. The host side is `fc00:1:1:0::1/64`, set up with udev rules installed for the run, and the board answers at `fe80::1` and `fc00:1:1:0::2`.

The link is IPv6, so IPv6 turned off, a firewall, a VPN or a poor cable will stop the flash here.

anchor: SSH: start the flashing script on the board
steps.title: Step 4: the host logs in over SSH and starts the script
steps.body:
Using `sshpass`, the host connects as root to the initrd, an account that exists only inside the RAM-booted initrd. It starts `l4t_flash_from_kernel.sh` on the board.

That script reads `initrd_flash.cfg` to learn what to write and where.

anchor: NFS: the board mounts the host's flash package
steps.title: Step 5: the board mounts the host's images over NFS
steps.body:
The host exports `tools/kernel_flash/` images over NFS (a network file system) and removes the export afterwards. The board mounts it and reads the images from it.

If a firewall blocks NFS, the board cannot read the package and the flash stops here.

steps.anchor: the board writes its own storage
steps.title: Step 6: the board writes both storage devices
steps.body:
The Linux on the Jetson writes the QSPI-NOR boot firmware (chains A and B), and on the SD card, NVMe or USB drive it writes the GPT, kernel, kernel-dtb, ESP and APP (the root filesystem).

The host just waits, and the log is saved in `Linux_for_Tegra/initrdlog/`.

anchor: "Success": the board reboots from the new media
steps.title: Step 7: success, cleanup and a reboot into the new system
steps.body:
When the board reports success, the host cleans up its udev rules and NFS export, and the board reboots from the new media.

The normal boot chain then runs: MB1, on to UEFI and L4TLauncher, then Linux and a login (see docs/01).

steps.title: Most failures are at steps 1, 3 and 5
steps.body:
No `0955:` device means the jumper, cable or port. A step 3 that never comes up points to IPv6 being off, a firewall, a VPN or a poor-quality cable. A step 5 failure usually means NFS is blocked by a firewall.

Details and fixes are in `docs/09-troubleshooting.md` and `docs/11-recovery-and-usb-flash.md`.
